methodological_rigor.justification: This is a single-center retrospective study of 30 heavily pretreated pediatric R/R high-risk neuroblastoma patients treated with extended dinutuximab beta plus chemotherapy. The core methodological weakness is the absence of a comparator arm (standard 5-cycle regimen or alternative therapy), so the incremental benefit of extending therapy beyond 5 cycles cannot be causally inferred. Selection bias is inherent (only those who tolerated >5 cycles were included) and the authors acknowledge this. Statistical methods (Kaplan-Meier with log-rank, Cox regression, 95% CIs, binomial CI for ORR) are appropriate for the design, but multivariate Cox is explicitly exploratory given only limited progression events. No power calculation is presented.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: Oxford LoE 4 as a single-arm retrospective case series without controls. Clinical relevance is high because R/R high-risk neuroblastoma has very poor prognosis and dinutuximab beta is a licensed standard; data informing optimal duration of immunotherapy are practically important for pediatric oncologists and generate hypotheses for prospective trials. Specific observations (38.5% best response after cycle 5, 2-year OS 94.7%, manageable toxicity) directly address a real clinical question, though without a control arm the findings are hypothesis-generating.

reporting_quality.justification: As a retrospective observational cohort, STROBE is the relevant standard. The paper defines inclusion/exclusion, treatment schedule, response criteria (revised INRC), AE grading (CTCAE v5.0), follow-up duration, and reports effect estimates with 95% CIs. Gaps relative to STROBE include no explicit flowchart of patient selection, minimal discussion of confounding/missing data handling, and no discussion of statistical power. No data-sharing statement or raw data repository is mentioned; individual patient-level response details are in a supplementary table.

novelty_literature.justification: The paper is an incremental confirmation of observations already reported by Wieczorek et al. (2023, reference 12, Poland/Germany) showing 31% best response after >5 cycles up to 10 cycles, and by Olgun et al. (2022, reference 19, Turkey) with treatment up to 14 cycles. The present study extends these observations to a Chinese single-center cohort with up to 12 cycles, with similar response (38.5% benefitting from extended cycles) and tolerability findings. It does not introduce a new methodology, mechanism, or paradigm, but adds corroborating real-world data.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is clearly written with a logical Methods/Results/Discussion structure. Response rates are consistently reported with 95% CIs at defined timepoints, and survival data with KM figures and stratification by CR status are presented. Tables I-IV organize baseline, treatment, response, and toxicity data effectively, and supplementary figures/tables are referenced. Some passages are repetitive (e.g., toxicity descriptions in results and discussion), but overall readability is good.

key_strengths: Addresses a clinically important question (optimal duration of dinutuximab beta) in a poor-prognosis pediatric population
Consistent response reporting with 95% CIs at prespecified timepoints (cycles 3, 5/6, end) and documented 38.5% of responders improving beyond cycle 5
Detailed toxicity reporting aligned with CTCAE v5.0 and SIOPEN experience; manageable AE profile with no immune-related deaths
Clinically useful imaging illustrations and individual-patient response tracking
key_concerns: Single-center retrospective design with no comparator arm prevents causal inference about benefit of extended cycles
Small sample (n=30, only 20 with residual disease evaluable for ORR) limits power and stability of subgroup estimates
Selection bias: inclusion requires having already completed >5 cycles, favoring tolerant/responding patients
Multivariate Cox analysis acknowledged as underpowered and hypothesis-generating only
Novelty limited given prior similar extended-cycle cohorts (Poland/Germany, Turkey) with comparable findings
chief_reviewer.rationale: A well-reported but design-limited retrospective cohort addressing an important practical question; fits a mid-tier specialty oncology journal after major revisions emphasizing the uncontrolled, hypothesis-generating nature of the findings.
